title: བསྟན་འགྱུར། སྡེ་དགེ། ཚད་མ། ཚེ (Derge Tengyur, vol. 187)
shelf_note: Derge woodblock folio of a pramāṇa commentary (universals, anvaya, the Devadatta 'either one eats' example); belongs in the Tengyur Pramāṇa section.

tr_errors_A.english: the statement that "either one is eating" carries the meaning: "Is the one slain, or..."
tr_errors_A.problem: The comparison ('it is like saying "shall [I] kill one or the other?"') is rendered awkwardly and opaquely; meaning is kept but hard to follow.

tr_errors_A.english: He states: "that also" and so forth. Regarding the phrase, "doubting because of the absence of positive concomitance"
tr_errors_A.problem: Faithful; 'ཟ་ལ' read as 'doubting' rather than 'is doubtful' — slight.

tr_errors_B.english: then the question "is one of them eating?" or "is it one or the other?" would be meaningless.
tr_errors_B.problem: The source says the phrase has the sense of 'shall [I] kill one or the other?'; B drops the 'kill' (སོད) comparison and invents 'would be meaningless'.

tr_errors_B.english: because this is an instance of considering the consciousness accompanied by a plurality.
tr_errors_B.problem: སེམས་པ here is the verb 'considering' (as in the preceding ཆོས་བསམ་པའི་སྐབས); B adds a spurious 'consciousness' object.

tr_errors_B.english: impossible for the body and the pot to be accompanied by a second <note>referring to a dual nature or a separate consciousness</note>
tr_errors_B.problem: Speculative explanatory note not grounded in the text; rendering of གཉིས་པ as 'a second' muddles the point.

tr_errors_B.english: If one asks why there is no separate object, the text says: "Since there is no positive pervasion, there is doubt."
tr_errors_B.problem: The lemma 'དེ་ཡང་' is dropped and merged into the next lemma.

pages.prefer_reason: A keeps the 'kill one or the other' comparison and reads སེམས་པ correctly as 'considering', where B replaces the comparison with an invented 'meaningless' and adds a spurious 'consciousness'.

book_verdict: Clean Derge pramāṇa folio with an OCR that matches the block print line for line; both translations follow the argument, A more faithfully than B, with no serious errors in either.
